
# Lecture 41.2: Compound Poisson Process

## Setting and Standing Assumptions

Throughout, $S$ is a countable set with the discrete $\sigma$-algebra $2^S$, and $B(S) = \ell_\infty(S)$ is the Banach space of bounded real-valued functions on $S$ with the supremum norm $\|f\|_\infty = \sup_{i \in S} |f(i)|$, as in Lecture 41.1. For a matrix $\Theta = (\Theta(i,j))_{i,j \in S}$ we write $\|\Theta\|_{\mathrm{row}} = \sup_{i} \sum_{j} |\Theta(i,j)|$ and, when $\|\Theta\|_{\mathrm{row}} < \infty$, $T_\Theta$ for the bounded operator $T_\Theta f(i) = \sum_j \Theta(i,j) f(j)$; recall $\|T_\Theta\|_{\mathrm{op}} = \|\Theta\|_{\mathrm{row}}$ (@lem-row-sum-norm). For an operator $T$ on $B(S)$ we write $T(i,j) \coloneqq T(\mathbf{1}_{\{j\}})(i)$ for its matrix entries.

Let $(q_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a family of transition probability mass functions on $S$ satisfying conditions 1–4 of Lecture 41.1 (non-negativity, unit row sums, $q_0(i,j) = \delta_{ij}$, and the Chapman–Kolmogorov equations), and let $Q_t = T_{q_t}$, so that $(Q_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a semigroup on $B(S)$ with $Q_0 = I$.

A process $(X_t)_{t \ge 0}$ of $S$-valued random variables on a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ is a **time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition function $(q_t)$ and initial law $\mu$** if for all $k \ge 0$, all $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_k$ and all $i_0, \dots, i_k \in S$,
$$
\mathbb{P}(X_{t_0} = i_0, X_{t_1} = i_1, \dots, X_{t_k} = i_k) = \mu(i_0) \prod_{\ell=1}^{k} q_{t_\ell - t_{\ell-1}}(i_{\ell-1}, i_\ell).
$$ {#eq-fdd-markov}
In particular, $\mathbb{P}(X_t = j \mid X_0 = i) = q_t(i,j)$ whenever $\mathbb{P}(X_0 = i) > 0$; the function $q_t(i,j)$ itself is defined for all $i$, independently of $\mu$.

## The Bounded Generator Case

Suppose $(Q_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is continuous in operator norm at $0$:
$$
\lim_{t \downarrow 0} \|Q_t - I\|_{\mathrm{op}} = 0,
$$
equivalently (@eq-uniform-condition, Lecture 41.1), $\lim_{t \downarrow 0} \inf_{i \in S} q_t(i,i) = 1$. By the generator theorem (@thm-bounded-generator, Lecture 40.2; see also @eq-semigroup-exp), the limit
$$
A = \lim_{t \downarrow 0} \frac{Q_t - I}{t}
$$
exists in operator norm, $A$ is a bounded linear operator on $B(S)$, and
$$
Q_t = e^{tA} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n!} A^n, \quad t \ge 0,
$$
with convergence in operator norm.

By @cor-generator-matrix (Lecture 41.1), the right derivatives
$$
a(i, j) = \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} q_t(i, j) \right|_{t=0^+} = \lim_{t \downarrow 0} \frac{q_t(i, j) - \delta_{ij}}{t}
$$
exist for all $i, j \in S$, $\|a\|_{\mathrm{row}} < \infty$, and $A$ is represented by the matrix $a$:
$$
(Af)(i) = \sum_{j \in S} a(i, j) f(j), \qquad f \in B(S),\ i \in S.
$$
(This is not automatic for an arbitrary bounded operator on $\ell_\infty(S)$, cf. @exm-banach-limit; it holds here because $A$ is the operator-norm limit of the matrix operators $(Q_t - I)/t$, @prp-operator-matrix-limit.) Moreover, by @cor-q-matrix-properties, $a(i,j) \ge 0$ for $i \ne j$, $a(i,i) \le 0$, $\sum_{j} a(i,j) = 0$ (absolutely convergent), and $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}} = \|a\|_{\mathrm{row}} = 2 \sup_i |a(i,i)| < \infty$.

The small-time expansion holds **uniformly** in $i, j \in S$: since $q_t(i,j) - \delta_{ij} - t a(i,j) = \bigl((e^{tA} - I - tA)\mathbf{1}_{\{j\}}\bigr)(i)$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sup_{i,j \in S} \bigl| q_t(i, j) - \delta_{ij} - t\, a(i, j) \bigr| &\le \|e^{tA} - I - tA\|_{\mathrm{op}} \\
& \le e^{t\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}} - 1 - t\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}} = O(t^2) \quad \text{as } t \downarrow 0.
\end{aligned}
$$
In particular, for $i \neq j$ and any Markov chain $(X_t)$ with transition function $(q_t)$ and $\mathbb{P}(X_0 = i) > 0$,
$$
\mathbb{P}(X_t = j \mid X_0 = i) = a(i, j)\, t + O(t^2) \quad \text{as } t \downarrow 0.
$$

::: {#def-bounded-rates}
## Conservative Q-Matrix with Bounded Rates
A matrix $a = (a(i,j))_{i,j \in S}$ is a **conservative Q-matrix** if $a(i,i) \in (-\infty, 0]$ for all $i$, $a(i,j) \ge 0$ for all $i \ne j$, and $\sum_{j \in S} a(i,j) = 0$ for all $i \in S$. It has **bounded rates** if, in addition,
$$
\sup_{i \in S} |a(i, i)| < \infty.
$$
:::

::: {#rem-bounded-rates}
## Bounded Rates and Operator-Norm Continuity
1. If $(q_t)$ satisfies conditions 1–4 and $\|Q_t - I\|_{\mathrm{op}} \to 0$, its generator matrix $a$ is a conservative Q-matrix with bounded rates (@cor-q-matrix-properties).
2. Conversely, every conservative Q-matrix $a$ with bounded rates generates the operator-norm continuous Markov semigroup $Q_t = e^{tT_a}$, whose generator matrix is $a$ (@thm-q-matrix-converse).
3. Statement 2 does **not** by itself say that *every* transition function whose derivatives at $0$ form a bounded-rate Q-matrix is operator-norm continuous; that requires an additional argument. For a *standard* transition function (i.e. $q_t(i,i) \to 1$ for each $i$) the derivatives $q_i \coloneqq -q'_{ii}(0^+) \in [0, \infty]$ always exist and satisfy $q_t(i,i) \ge e^{-q_i t}$ (Kolmogorov; see e.g. Chung, *Markov Chains with Stationary Transition Probabilities*, §II.2, or Anderson, *Continuous-Time Markov Chains*, Ch. 1). Granting this, if $\sup_i q_i < \infty$ then $1 - q_t(i,i) \le q_i t \le t \sup_k q_k$, so $\inf_i q_t(i,i) \to 1$, i.e. $\|Q_t - I\|_{\mathrm{op}} \to 0$ by @eq-uniform-condition. We do not prove the inequality $q_t(i,i) \ge e^{-q_i t}$ here.
:::

::: {#lem-generator-bounds}
## Total Absolute Rate per Row
Let $a$ be a conservative Q-matrix. Then for every $i \in S$,
$$
\sum_{j \in S} |a(i, j)| = 2 |a(i, i)|,
$$
and consequently
$$
\|a\|_{\mathrm{row}} = \sup_{i \in S} \sum_{j \in S} |a(i, j)| = 2 \sup_{i \in S} |a(i, i)| \in [0, \infty].
$$ {#eq-rate-bound}
In particular, $\|a\|_{\mathrm{row}} < \infty$ if and only if $a$ has bounded rates, in which case $T_a$ is a bounded operator with $\|T_a\|_{\mathrm{op}} = 2 \sup_i |a(i,i)|$ (@lem-row-sum-norm).
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @lem-generator-bounds
Fix $i \in S$. Since $a(i,i)$ is finite and $\sum_j a(i,j) = 0$, we have $\sum_{j \ne i} a(i,j) = -a(i,i) = |a(i,i)|$, the series having non-negative terms. Hence
$$
\sum_{j \in S} |a(i, j)| = |a(i, i)| + \sum_{j \neq i} a(i, j) = 2 |a(i, i)|.
$$
Taking the supremum over $i \in S$ yields @eq-rate-bound (both sides possibly $+\infty$). Without the bounded-rates assumption the supremum may be infinite: on $S = \mathbb{N}$, the conservative Q-matrix with $a(i,i) = -i$, $a(i,i+1) = i$ and all other entries $0$ has $\|a\|_{\mathrm{row}} = \infty$.
:::

---

## Uniformization (Randomization) Construction

By @eq-fdd-markov, the finite-dimensional distributions of a Markov chain are determined by its initial law $\mu$ and its transition function; in the bounded case the transition function is $q_t(i,j) = e^{tA}(i,j)$, so it is determined by the generator matrix $a$. We now construct such a chain by running a discrete-time Markov chain at the jump times of an independent Poisson process.

## Rescaling and the Stochastic Transition Matrix

Let $a$ be a conservative Q-matrix with bounded rates, $A = T_a$, and let $\lambda$ be a constant with
$$
\lambda > 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \lambda \ge \sup_{i \in S} |a(i, i)| = \tfrac{1}{2} \|A\|_{\mathrm{op}},
$$
where the equality is @eq-rate-bound together with @lem-row-sum-norm. Define the matrix $p$ and the operator $P$ by
$$
p(i,j) = \delta_{ij} + \frac{1}{\lambda} a(i,j), \qquad P = T_p = I + \frac{1}{\lambda} A.
$$ {#eq-stochastic-matrix-def}
(The second identity holds because $T_\delta = I$ and $\Theta \mapsto T_\Theta$ is linear, @lem-row-sum-norm.)

::: {#lem-markov-matrix}
## Properties of $P$
Under the above assumptions, $p$ is a (row-)stochastic matrix, i.e. $p(i,j) \ge 0$ and $\sum_{j} p(i,j) = 1$ for all $i, j \in S$. Consequently $P$ is a positivity-preserving bounded operator on $B(S)$ with $P\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$ and $\|P\|_{\mathrm{op}} = 1$.
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @lem-markov-matrix
1. **Non-negativity:** For $i \neq j$, $p(i, j) = \frac{1}{\lambda} a(i, j) \ge 0$. For $i = j$, since $a(i,i) \le 0$,
   $$
   p(i, i) = 1 + \frac{1}{\lambda} a(i, i) = 1 - \frac{|a(i, i)|}{\lambda} \ge 0,
   $$
   because $|a(i,i)| \le \sup_k |a(k,k)| \le \lambda$.
2. **Row sums:** For every $i \in S$, the series $\sum_j a(i,j)$ converges absolutely (@lem-generator-bounds), so the sum may be split:
   $$
   \sum_{j \in S} p(i, j) = \sum_{j \in S} \delta_{ij} + \frac{1}{\lambda} \sum_{j \in S} a(i, j) = 1 + 0 = 1.
   $$
3. **Norm:** By 1–2, $\|p\|_{\mathrm{row}} = \sup_i \sum_j p(i,j) = 1$, so $\|P\|_{\mathrm{op}} = 1$ by @lem-row-sum-norm; positivity and $P\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}$ are immediate from 1–2.
:::

By the Kolmogorov extension theorem (Lectures 16.1–16.2), for every probability measure $\mu$ on $S$ there exists a discrete-time Markov chain $(Y_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0}$ with initial law $\mu$ and transition matrix $p$, i.e.
$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_0 = i_0, Y_1 = i_1, \dots, Y_n = i_n) = \mu(i_0) \prod_{\ell=1}^{n} p(i_{\ell-1}, i_\ell), 
$$
for $n \ge 0$ and $i_0, \dots, i_n \in S$. Summing over intermediate states (all sums have non-negative terms) gives, for $0 = n_0 \le n_1 \le \dots \le n_k$,
$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_0 = i_0, Y_{n_1} = i_1, \dots, Y_{n_k} = i_k) = \mu(i_0) \prod_{\ell=1}^{k} p^{(n_\ell - n_{\ell-1})}(i_{\ell-1}, i_\ell),
$$ {#eq-y-fdd}
where $p^{(m)}$ is the $m$-th matrix power of $p$ ($p^{(0)}(i,j) = \delta_{ij}$). As shown in the proof of @thm-q-matrix-converse, $P^m = T_{p^{(m)}}$, i.e. $P^m(i,j) = p^{(m)}(i,j)$.

---

## The Main Uniformization Theorem

For $\theta \ge 0$ write $\pi_\theta(m) = e^{-\theta} \theta^m / m!$, $m \in \mathbb{N}_0$, for the Poisson($\theta$) probability mass function.

::: {#thm-uniformization}
## Main Uniformization Theorem
Let $a$ be a conservative Q-matrix with bounded rates on a countable set $S$, let $A = T_a$, and fix $\lambda > 0$ with $\lambda \ge \sup_{i \in S} |a(i, i)|$. Let $p$ and $P$ be as in @eq-stochastic-matrix-def. On a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ let:

1. $(Y_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0}$ be a discrete-time Markov chain on $S$ with initial law $\mu$ and transition matrix $p$;
2. $(N_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ (as defined in Lecture 38.1): $N_0 = 0$; for $0 = s_0 < s_1 < \dots < s_k$ the increments $N_{s_1} - N_{s_0}, \dots, N_{s_k} - N_{s_{k-1}}$ are independent; and $N_t - N_s \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s))$ for $0 \le s < t$. We assume, modifying $N$ on a null set if necessary, that **every** path $t \mapsto N_t(\omega)$ is $\mathbb{N}_0$-valued and non-decreasing with $N_0(\omega) = 0$;
3. the processes $(Y_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0}$ and $(N_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be independent, i.e. $\sigma(Y_n : n \in \mathbb{N}_0)$ and $\sigma(N_t : t \ge 0)$ are independent.

Then $X_t \coloneqq Y_{N_t}$, $t \ge 0$, defines $S$-valued random variables, and $(X_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a time-homogeneous Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition function
$$
q_t(i,j) = e^{tA}(i,j), \qquad e^{tA} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \pi_{\lambda t}(n) P^n,
$$
whose generator is $A = \lambda(P - I)$ and whose generator matrix is $a$. In particular, for all $s, t \ge 0$ and $f \in B(S)$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\bigl[f(X_{t+s}) \mid \mathcal{F}^X_t\bigr] = (e^{sA} f)(X_t) \quad \text{a.s.}, \qquad \mathcal{F}^X_t \coloneqq \sigma(X_r : 0 \le r \le t).
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @thm-uniformization
### Step 0: Measurability
Since every $N_t(\omega) \in \mathbb{N}_0$, for each $j \in S$
$$
\{X_t = j\} = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0} \{Y_n = j\} \cap \{N_t = n\} \in \mathcal{F},
$$
so $X_t$ is a random variable. Also $X_0 = Y_{N_0} = Y_0$, so $X_0 \sim \mu$.

### Step 1: The Semigroup Representation
By @eq-stochastic-matrix-def, $A = \lambda(P - I) = \lambda P - \lambda I$. Since $\lambda I$ commutes with $\lambda P$, $e^{tA} = e^{-\lambda t I} e^{\lambda t P} = e^{-\lambda t} e^{\lambda t P}$, hence
$$
e^{tA} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} e^{-\lambda t} \frac{(\lambda t)^n}{n!} P^n = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \pi_{\lambda t}(n)\, P^n,
$$ {#eq-semigroup-expansion}
the series converging in operator norm because $\|P^n\|_{\mathrm{op}} \le 1$. Evaluating at $\mathbf{1}_{\{j\}}$ and at $i$,
$$
e^{tA}(i,j) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \pi_{\lambda t}(n)\, p^{(n)}(i,j).
$$ {#eq-semigroup-entries}
By @thm-q-matrix-converse, $q_t(i,j) \coloneqq e^{tA}(i,j)$ satisfies conditions 1–4 of Lecture 41.1, $e^{tA} = T_{q_t}$, and its generator matrix is $a$.

### Step 2: Finite-Dimensional Distributions
Fix $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_k$ and $i_0, \dots, i_k \in S$, and put $n_0 = 0$. Since every path of $N$ is $\mathbb{N}_0$-valued, non-decreasing, and starts at $0$, the events $\{N_{t_1} = n_1, \dots, N_{t_k} = n_k\}$, $0 \le n_1 \le \dots \le n_k$, partition $\Omega$, and on such an event $X_{t_\ell} = Y_{n_\ell}$. By countable additivity and the independence in hypothesis 3,
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{P}(X_{t_0} = i_0, \dots, X_{t_k} = i_k) \\
& = \sum_{0 \le n_1 \le \dots \le n_k} \mathbb{P}(Y_0 = i_0, Y_{n_1} = i_1, \dots, Y_{n_k} = i_k)\, \mathbb{P}(N_{t_1} = n_1, \dots, N_{t_k} = n_k).
\end{aligned}
$$
Set $m_\ell = n_\ell - n_{\ell-1}$; the map $(n_1, \dots, n_k) \mapsto (m_1, \dots, m_k)$ is a bijection from $\{0 \le n_1 \le \dots \le n_k\}$ onto $\mathbb{N}_0^k$. By the independence of the increments and their Poisson laws (hypothesis 2),
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(N_{t_1} = n_1, \dots, N_{t_k} = n_k) &= \mathbb{P}\bigl(N_{t_\ell} - N_{t_{\ell-1}} = m_\ell,\ \ell = 1, \dots, k\bigr) \\
& = \prod_{\ell=1}^{k} \pi_{\lambda(t_\ell - t_{\ell-1})}(m_\ell),
\end{aligned}
$$
and by @eq-y-fdd,
$\mathbb{P}(Y_0 = i_0, Y_{n_1} = i_1, \dots, Y_{n_k} = i_k) = \mu(i_0) \prod_{\ell=1}^{k} p^{(m_\ell)}(i_{\ell-1}, i_\ell)$. Since all terms are non-negative, the sum over $\mathbb{N}_0^k$ of a product factorizes (Tonelli for counting measure), and by @eq-semigroup-entries
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X_{t_0} = i_0, \dots, X_{t_k} = i_k) &= \mu(i_0) \prod_{\ell=1}^{k} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \pi_{\lambda(t_\ell - t_{\ell-1})}(m)\, p^{(m)}(i_{\ell-1}, i_\ell) \\
& = \mu(i_0) \prod_{\ell=1}^{k} q_{t_\ell - t_{\ell-1}}(i_{\ell-1}, i_\ell).
\end{aligned}
$$
This is @eq-fdd-markov, so $(X_t)$ is a time-homogeneous Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition function $(q_t)$.

### Step 3: The Markov Property
Fix $t \ge 0$, $s > 0$ (the case $s = 0$ is trivial) and $f \in B(S)$. Let $\mathcal{C}_t$ be the collection consisting of $\Omega$ and all cylinder events $C = \{X_{r_1} = j_1, \dots, X_{r_m} = j_m\}$ with $m \ge 1$, $r_1, \dots, r_m \in [0, t]$ and $j_1, \dots, j_m \in S$. Then $\mathcal{C}_t$ is a $\pi$-system (the intersection of two cylinder events is a cylinder event or $\emptyset = \{X_0 = j\} \cap \{X_0 = j'\}$ for $j \ne j'$) generating $\mathcal{F}^X_t$.

*Claim:* $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_C f(X_{t+s})] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_C (Q_s f)(X_t)]$ for all $C \in \mathcal{C}_t$. Writing $C$ as a countable disjoint union over the values of $X_0$ and $X_t$ (and both sides are countably additive in $C$, being integrals of bounded functions), it suffices to treat $C = \{X_{r_0} = j_0, \dots, X_{r_m} = j_m\}$ with $0 = r_0 < r_1 < \dots < r_m = t$ (if $t = 0$, $m = 0$). By Step 2 applied to the times $r_0 < \dots < r_m < t + s$,
$$
\mathbb{P}(C \cap \{X_{t+s} = j\}) = \mathbb{P}(C)\, q_s(j_m, j), \qquad j \in S.
$$
Multiplying by $f(j)$ and summing over $j$ (absolutely convergent, since $\sum_j \mathbb{P}(C \cap \{X_{t+s} = j\}) = \mathbb{P}(C)$ and $f$ is bounded),
$$
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_C f(X_{t+s})] = \mathbb{P}(C)\, (Q_s f)(j_m) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_C (Q_s f)(X_t)].
$$
The class of $C \in \mathcal{F}^X_t$ satisfying the claimed identity is a $\lambda$-system (both sides are finite signed measures in $C$), so by Dynkin's $\pi$–$\lambda$ theorem it contains $\mathcal{F}^X_t$. Since $(Q_s f)(X_t)$ is $\mathcal{F}^X_t$-measurable and bounded, this proves $\mathbb{E}[f(X_{t+s}) \mid \mathcal{F}^X_t] = (Q_s f)(X_t)$ a.s. with $Q_s = e^{sA}$.
:::

---

## Filtration Construction

The process $X$ is Markov with respect to its natural filtration by @thm-uniformization. The following result, which is formulated in Driver's lecture notes (Thm. 22.34), shows that it is Markov with respect to a larger filtration that carries the full information of $Y$ up to the current number of jumps and of $N$ up to the current time. Here $p$ may be **any** stochastic matrix on $S$.

::: {#thm-driver-filtration}
## Explicit Filtration Construction (Driver, Thm 22.34)
Let $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, (\mathcal{F}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0}, \mathbb{P})$ be a filtered probability space and let $p$ be a stochastic matrix on the countable set $S$, with $P = T_p$. Assume:

1. $(Y_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0}$ is an $(\mathcal{F}_n)$-adapted, $S$-valued process that is Markov **with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$** with transition matrix $p$:
   $$
   \mathbb{P}(Y_{n+1} = j \mid \mathcal{F}_n) = p(Y_n, j) \quad \text{a.s.}, \qquad n \in \mathbb{N}_0,\ j \in S;
   $$
2. $(N_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a Poisson process with rate $\lambda > 0$ as in hypothesis 2 of @thm-uniformization (in particular every path is $\mathbb{N}_0$-valued, non-decreasing, with $N_0 = 0$);
3. the $\sigma$-algebra $\sigma(N_t : t \ge 0)$ is independent of
   $$
   \mathcal{F}_\infty \coloneqq \sigma\Bigl(\bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}_0} \mathcal{F}_n\Bigr).
   $$
   (Note that $\mathcal{F}_\infty$ is the *terminal* $\sigma$-algebra of the filtration, not the tail $\sigma$-algebra $\bigcap_n \sigma(Y_m : m \ge n)$; independence from the latter would not suffice.)

Let $\mathcal{F}^N_t \coloneqq \sigma(N_r : 0 \le r \le t)$ and define, for $t \ge 0$,
$$
\mathcal{G}_t \coloneqq \Bigl\{ B \in \mathcal{F} :\ B \cap \{N_t = n\} \in \mathcal{F}_n \vee \mathcal{F}^N_t \ \text{ for all } n \in \mathbb{N}_0 \Bigr\},
$$ {#eq-gt-filtration}
where $\mathcal{F}_n \vee \mathcal{F}^N_t = \sigma(\mathcal{F}_n \cup \mathcal{F}^N_t)$. Let $X_t \coloneqq Y_{N_t}$ and $Q_s \coloneqq e^{\lambda s (P - I)}$. Then:

1. $(\mathcal{G}_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a filtration on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$.
2. $(X_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is adapted to $(\mathcal{G}_t)_{t \ge 0}$; in particular $\mathcal{F}^X_t \subseteq \mathcal{G}_t$.
3. $(X_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a time-homogeneous Markov process relative to $(\mathcal{G}_t)_{t \ge 0}$ with transition operators $(Q_s)_{s \ge 0}$: for all $s, t \ge 0$ and $f \in B(S)$,
   $$
   \mathbb{E}[f(X_{t+s}) \mid \mathcal{G}_t] = (Q_s f)(X_t) \quad \text{a.s.}
   $$
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @thm-driver-filtration
Throughout, $P^m = T_{p^{(m)}}$ (see the discussion after @lem-markov-matrix), and hypothesis 1 implies, by induction on $m$ and the tower property,
$$
\mathbb{E}[f(Y_{n+m}) \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = (P^m f)(Y_n) \quad \text{a.s.}, \qquad n, m \in \mathbb{N}_0,\ f \in B(S).
$$ {#eq-y-markov-m}
As in Step 1 of the proof of @thm-uniformization (which used only $\|P\|_{\mathrm{op}} = 1$), $Q_s = \sum_{m \ge 0} \pi_{\lambda s}(m) P^m$ in operator norm, hence pointwise.

1. **Filtration property.** *$\mathcal{G}_t$ is a $\sigma$-algebra:* $\Omega \in \mathcal{G}_t$ since $\{N_t = n\} \in \mathcal{F}^N_t$; if $B \in \mathcal{G}_t$ then $B^c \cap \{N_t = n\} = \{N_t = n\} \setminus (B \cap \{N_t = n\}) \in \mathcal{F}_n \vee \mathcal{F}^N_t$; and countable unions commute with intersecting by $\{N_t = n\}$.

   *Monotonicity:* let $s \le t$ and $B \in \mathcal{G}_s$. Since every path of $N$ is $\mathbb{N}_0$-valued and non-decreasing, $\{N_t = n\} \subseteq \{N_s \le n\}$, so
   $$
   B \cap \{N_t = n\} = \bigcup_{m=0}^{n} \bigl(B \cap \{N_s = m\}\bigr) \cap \{N_t = n\}.
   $$
   Each $B \cap \{N_s = m\}$ lies in $\mathcal{F}_m \vee \mathcal{F}^N_s \subseteq \mathcal{F}_n \vee \mathcal{F}^N_t$ (as $m \le n$ and $s \le t$), and $\{N_t = n\} \in \mathcal{F}^N_t$. Hence $B \cap \{N_t = n\} \in \mathcal{F}_n \vee \mathcal{F}^N_t$ for all $n$, i.e. $B \in \mathcal{G}_t$.

2. **Adaptedness.** For $E \subseteq S$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$,
   $$
   \{X_t \in E\} \cap \{N_t = n\} = \{Y_n \in E\} \cap \{N_t = n\} \in \mathcal{F}_n \vee \mathcal{F}^N_t,
   $$
   because $Y_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable and $\{N_t = n\} \in \mathcal{F}^N_t$. Also $\{X_t \in E\} = \bigcup_n \{Y_n \in E\} \cap \{N_t = n\} \in \mathcal{F}$. Thus $\{X_t \in E\} \in \mathcal{G}_t$. Since $(\mathcal{G}_t)$ is a filtration, $\mathcal{F}^X_t \subseteq \mathcal{G}_t$.

3. **Markov property.** Fix $s, t \ge 0$, $f \in B(S)$, and for $m \in \mathbb{N}_0$ let $D_m \coloneqq \{N_{t+s} - N_t = m\}$, so that $\mathbb{P}(D_m) = \pi_{\lambda s}(m)$.

   *Step (a).* For all $n, m \in \mathbb{N}_0$ and $C \in \mathcal{F}_n \vee \mathcal{F}^N_t$:
   $$
   \mathbb{E}\bigl[f(Y_{n+m}) \mathbf{1}_C \mathbf{1}_{D_m}\bigr] = \mathbb{E}\bigl[(P^m f)(Y_n) \mathbf{1}_C\bigr]\, \mathbb{P}(D_m).
   $$ {#eq-key-identity}
   First let $C = F \cap G$ with $F \in \mathcal{F}_n$, $G \in \mathcal{F}^N_t$. The variables $f(Y_{n+m}) \mathbf{1}_F$ and $(P^m f)(Y_n) \mathbf{1}_F$ are bounded and $\mathcal{F}_\infty$-measurable, while $\mathbf{1}_G$ and $\mathbf{1}_G \mathbf{1}_{D_m}$ are $\sigma(N_r : r \ge 0)$-measurable. By hypothesis 3, then the independence of $D_m$ from $\mathcal{F}^N_t$ (the increment $N_{t+s} - N_t$ is independent of $(N_{r_1}, \dots, N_{r_k})$ for all $r_1, \dots, r_k \le t$ by independent increments, and hence of $\mathcal{F}^N_t$ by a $\pi$–$\lambda$ argument), then @eq-y-markov-m, then hypothesis 3 again:
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   \mathbb{E}[f(Y_{n+m}) \mathbf{1}_F \mathbf{1}_G \mathbf{1}_{D_m}] &= \mathbb{E}[f(Y_{n+m}) \mathbf{1}_F]\, \mathbb{P}(G \cap D_m) \\
   & = \mathbb{E}[f(Y_{n+m}) \mathbf{1}_F]\, \mathbb{P}(G)\, \mathbb{P}(D_m) \\
   &= \mathbb{E}[(P^m f)(Y_n) \mathbf{1}_F]\, \mathbb{P}(G)\, \mathbb{P}(D_m) \\
   &= \mathbb{E}[(P^m f)(Y_n) \mathbf{1}_F \mathbf{1}_G]\, \mathbb{P}(D_m).
   \end{aligned}
   $$
   The sets $F \cap G$ form a $\pi$-system containing $\Omega$ and generating $\mathcal{F}_n \vee \mathcal{F}^N_t$. Both sides of @eq-key-identity are finite signed measures in $C$ (as $f$ is bounded), so the class of $C$ satisfying @eq-key-identity is a $\lambda$-system, and Dynkin's $\pi$–$\lambda$ theorem gives @eq-key-identity for all $C \in \mathcal{F}_n \vee \mathcal{F}^N_t$.

   *Step (b).* Let $B \in \mathcal{G}_t$. Since $N_t$ and $N_{t+s} - N_t$ are $\mathbb{N}_0$-valued everywhere, the events $\{N_t = n\} \cap D_m$, $n, m \in \mathbb{N}_0$, partition $\Omega$, and on $\{N_t = n\} \cap D_m$ we have $X_{t+s} = Y_{n+m}$. Applying @eq-key-identity with $C = B \cap \{N_t = n\} \in \mathcal{F}_n \vee \mathcal{F}^N_t$ and using dominated convergence ($f$ bounded) to interchange sums and expectations,
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   \mathbb{E}[f(X_{t+s}) \mathbf{1}_B] &= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{E}\bigl[f(Y_{n+m}) \mathbf{1}_{B \cap \{N_t = n\}} \mathbf{1}_{D_m}\bigr] \\
   &= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \pi_{\lambda s}(m)\, \mathbb{E}\bigl[(P^m f)(Y_n) \mathbf{1}_{B \cap \{N_t = n\}}\bigr] \\
   &= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{E}\bigl[(Q_s f)(Y_n) \mathbf{1}_{B \cap \{N_t = n\}}\bigr] \\
   & = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \mathbb{E}\bigl[(Q_s f)(X_t) \mathbf{1}_{B \cap \{N_t = n\}}\bigr] \\
   &= \mathbb{E}\bigl[(Q_s f)(X_t) \mathbf{1}_B\bigr].
   \end{aligned}
   $$
   The interchange of $\sum_m$ and $\mathbb{E}$ is justified by $\sum_m \pi_{\lambda s}(m) \|P^m f\|_\infty \le \|f\|_\infty$. Since $(Q_s f)(X_t)$ is bounded and $\mathcal{G}_t$-measurable by part 2, this proves $\mathbb{E}[f(X_{t+s}) \mid \mathcal{G}_t] = (Q_s f)(X_t)$ a.s.
:::

::: {#rem-filtration-consistency}
## Consistency with @thm-uniformization
If $p = \delta + a/\lambda$ as in @eq-stochastic-matrix-def, then $Q_s = e^{s A}$ with $A = \lambda(P - I) = T_a$. Taking $\mathcal{F}_n = \sigma(Y_0, \dots, Y_n)$, hypothesis 3 of @thm-driver-filtration is hypothesis 3 of @thm-uniformization, and conditioning the conclusion of @thm-driver-filtration on $\mathcal{F}^X_t \subseteq \mathcal{G}_t$ (tower property) recovers the Markov property in @thm-uniformization.
:::

---

## The Compound Poisson Process

::: {#def-compound-poisson}
## Compound Poisson Process
Let $d \ge 1$, let $\nu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb{Z}^d$, and let $\lambda > 0$. On a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ let $Y_0$ be a $\mathbb{Z}^d$-valued random variable with law $\mu$, let $(\xi_k)_{k \ge 1}$ be i.i.d. with law $\nu$, and let $(N_t)_{t \ge 0}$ be a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ as in hypothesis 2 of @thm-uniformization, such that $Y_0$, $(\xi_k)_{k \ge 1}$ and $(N_t)_{t \ge 0}$ are independent. The process
$$
X_t \coloneqq Y_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{N_t} \xi_k, \qquad t \ge 0,
$$
is a **compound Poisson process** with rate $\lambda$, jump distribution $\nu$, and initial law $\mu$.
:::

With $Y_n \coloneqq Y_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \xi_k$ (a random walk with step law $\nu$), we have $X_t = Y_{N_t}$: the compound Poisson process is exactly the uniformization of a random walk.

::: {#prp-compound-poisson-markov}
## Compound Poisson Processes are Uniformized Chains
In the setting of @def-compound-poisson, let $S = \mathbb{Z}^d$ and define
$$
a(i, j) \coloneqq \lambda \bigl(\nu(\{j - i\}) - \delta_{ij}\bigr), \qquad i, j \in \mathbb{Z}^d.
$$
Then $a$ is a conservative Q-matrix with bounded rates, $\sup_i |a(i,i)| = \lambda(1 - \nu(\{0\})) \le \lambda$, and $(X_t)_{t \ge 0}$ is a time-homogeneous Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition function $q_t(i,j) = e^{tA}(i,j)$, where $A = T_a$ acts by
$$
(Af)(i) = \lambda \sum_{j \in \mathbb{Z}^d} \nu(\{j\}) \bigl(f(i + j) - f(i)\bigr), \qquad f \in B(\mathbb{Z}^d),\ i \in \mathbb{Z}^d.
$$
Moreover, $X$ is Markov with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{G}_t)$ of @thm-driver-filtration built from $\mathcal{F}_n \coloneqq \sigma(Y_0, \xi_1, \dots, \xi_n)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
## Proof of @prp-compound-poisson-markov
*Q-matrix.* For $i \ne j$, $a(i,j) = \lambda \nu(\{j - i\}) \ge 0$; $a(i,i) = -\lambda(1 - \nu(\{0\})) \in [-\lambda, 0]$; and $\sum_j a(i,j) = \lambda\bigl(\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}^d} \nu(\{k\}) - 1\bigr) = 0$. Thus $a$ is a conservative Q-matrix with $\sup_i |a(i,i)| = \lambda(1 - \nu(\{0\})) \le \lambda$, and the formula for $Af$ follows from $Af(i) = \sum_j a(i,j) f(j)$ by the substitution $j \mapsto i + j$ (absolutely convergent).

*Random walk.* The matrix of @eq-stochastic-matrix-def is $p(i,j) = \delta_{ij} + a(i,j)/\lambda = \nu(\{j - i\})$. With $\mathcal{F}_n = \sigma(Y_0, \xi_1, \dots, \xi_n)$, $Y_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable and $\xi_{n+1}$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_n$, so
$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_{n+1} = j \mid \mathcal{F}_n) = \mathbb{P}(\xi_{n+1} = j - i)\big|_{i = Y_n} = p(Y_n, j) \quad \text{a.s.}
$$
Hence $(Y_n)$ is Markov with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ with transition matrix $p$ and initial law $\mu$; in particular it satisfies the finite-dimensional formula preceding @eq-y-fdd.

*Independence.* $\sigma(Y_n : n \ge 0) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_\infty = \sigma(Y_0, \xi_1, \xi_2, \dots)$, which is independent of $\sigma(N_t : t \ge 0)$ by assumption.

All hypotheses of @thm-uniformization (with this $\lambda$) and of @thm-driver-filtration are therefore satisfied, and both conclusions apply to $X_t = Y_{N_t}$.
:::

::: {#rem-fictitious-jumps}
## Fictitious Jumps
If $\nu(\{0\}) > 0$, some Poisson arrivals produce a "jump" of size $0$, so $X$ does not move. The same phenomenon occurs in general uniformization whenever $\lambda > |a(i,i)|$: then $p(i,i) > 0$, and at an arrival of $N$ the chain stays at $i$ with probability $p(i,i)$. The actual jump rate out of $i$ is $\lambda(1 - p(i,i)) = |a(i,i)|$, which does not depend on the choice of $\lambda$.
:::

---

## Takeaways

- For a Markov chain on a countable state space with operator-norm continuous semigroup, the generator $A$ is represented by a conservative Q-matrix $a$ with bounded rates, $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}} = 2 \sup_i |a(i,i)|$, and $q_t(i,j) = \delta_{ij} + t\, a(i,j) + O(t^2)$ uniformly in $i, j$.
- **Uniformization:** for any $\lambda > 0$ with $\lambda \ge \sup_i |a(i,i)|$, the matrix $p = \delta + a/\lambda$ is stochastic and $e^{tA} = \sum_n \pi_{\lambda t}(n) P^n$. Running a $p$-chain $Y$ at the arrival times of an independent rate-$\lambda$ Poisson process gives $X_t = Y_{N_t}$, a Markov chain with transition function $e^{tA}$.
- With the right hypotheses (Markov with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$, and $N$ independent of $\mathcal{F}_\infty$), $X$ is Markov with respect to the larger filtration $\mathcal{G}_t$ of @eq-gt-filtration, not only its natural filtration.
- A compound Poisson process on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ is the uniformization of a random walk. Its generator is $Af(i) = \lambda \sum_j \nu(\{j\})(f(i+j) - f(i))$.
